items.question: Your layout passed review at 375px and 768px, but a bug report shows it broken at 600px in landscape. You tested phone and tablet widths. What did the testing strategy miss?
items.answer: Breakpoints are snapshots, not guarantees. The layout has to hold at every width between and beyond the checked points: fluid sizing must carry the intermediate range, and any component that needs its own breakpoint should get one via a container query instead of inheriting the page's device breakpoints. Re-validate at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths, in both orientations, with real content.
items.trap: The naive belief is that validating the two most common device widths validates the layout. A layout tuned only at two snapshots can still fail at every width between them, which is exactly where landscape phones and small tablets live.

items.question: CrUX says the site's Web Vitals are good overall. Why is that still not enough to conclude that mobile users have a good experience?
items.answer: Because an aggregate can hide the mobile population. The Core Web Vitals guidance explicitly recommends segmenting results by mobile and desktop: a combined score can pass while mobile sessions, on slower devices and networks, fail. Report mobile separately, against the recommended thresholds at the recommended percentile, before claiming the mobile experience is good.
items.trap: The naive move is reading one aggregate score and assuming it represents everyone. Desktop sessions typically pull the aggregate up, so a passing blended score can coexist with a failing mobile experience.

items.question: To stop the page from scrolling during a drag, a teammate calls event.preventDefault() inside every pointermove handler. The page still scrolls on touch. Why, and what is the correct tool?
items.answer: With Pointer Events, whether the browser may pan or zoom a region is decided by the region's touch-action property, not by cancelling inside the move handler. Declare what the region owns: touch-action: none on a drag handle, or pan-y when vertical scrolling should stay available while horizontal drags are custom. Cancelling everything globally is precisely the anti-pattern to avoid.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that preventDefault in a pointer handler cancels scrolling the way it can in non-passive touch handlers. It does not control browser panning; without a touch-action declaration the browser is free to take over the gesture, which then surfaces as pointercancel.

items.question: A drag ends and your cleanup never runs: there was no pointerup. What happened, and what must the code do about it?
items.answer: The browser took over the gesture for its own panning or zooming and fired pointercancel instead. The code must treat pointercancel as a first-class end state: reset the drag, release pointer capture if it is held, and stop move handling. If pointercancel is ignored, the element is left stuck in a dragging state until the next pointerdown.
items.trap: The naive implementation only cleans up on pointerup. On touch, the OS and browser can reclaim the gesture at any moment, so a drag that only knows the happy path leaks state exactly when the user needs the page to behave normally.

items.question: Lighthouse reports all green in the lab, yet field data shows mobile users failing INP. The team proposes shipping anyway because the lab proves the code is fast. What is wrong with that argument?
items.answer: Lab and field answer different questions. The lab runs a scripted visit under a chosen device and network profile; field data is what real mobile users actually experienced. The correct workflow is to segment the field data by mobile device and route, use lab tooling to reproduce and explain the likely cause, ship the fix, and confirm in field data again. Real-user monitoring stays on permanently because lab results are not a substitute for field measurement.
items.trap: The naive belief is that a passing lab run certifies performance. Lab conditions rarely match the population of devices, networks, and interaction patterns that produced the field data, so the regression stays invisible in the lab until you deliberately reproduce it.

items.question: Why are the Core Web Vitals thresholds evaluated at the 75th percentile of visits rather than the median or the maximum?
items.answer: The recommended evaluation point is the 75th percentile: passing there means the large majority of visits, including a substantial share of the worse ones, met the threshold. A median only describes a typical session and says nothing about how bad the worse half is; a maximum is governed by a single worst outlier. The 75th percentile is the chosen compromise between representing real users and not being held hostage by outliers.
items.trap: The naive answer treats an average or median as the user experience. A median can look good while half the mobile sessions are slow, which is exactly the population the vitals thresholds are meant to protect.

items.question: selectedId changes in the parent, data does not, and half the rows in the FlatList never re-render to show the new selection. The team proposes forcing it with keyExtractor={(item) => item.id + '-' + selectedId}. Why is that wrong, and what is the right fix?
items.answer: FlatList is a PureComponent, so it only re-renders when its props change; a value that affects rows but lives outside data must arrive as a changed prop, which is exactly what extraData is for: pass extraData={selectedId}. Baking selection into the key is worse than the bug. Keys identify items across renders, so changing them remounts the affected rows, discarding row state and animations and breaking identity-based optimizations.
items.trap: The naive instinct is that keys are a general make-it-rerender lever. Keys are identity: changing them destroys and recreates rows instead of updating them, so the fix trades a missed update for remount churn and lost row state.

items.question: You add getItemLayout to skip measurement, and scrolling gets worse: fast scrolls land on the wrong rows and content overlaps. What happened?
items.answer: getItemLayout is only valid when row geometry is truly uniform. If any row can be taller than the declared length, for example text that wraps to extra lines, every offset after it is wrong: the list scrolls to computed positions that no longer match reality, and it skipped the measurement that would have corrected it. Either guarantee fixed heights by constraining row content, or remove getItemLayout and let the list measure.
items.trap: The naive reading is that getItemLayout is a free optimization. It is a contract: the moment one row violates the declared geometry, the list confidently scrolls to wrong offsets, which looks like a rendering bug but is actually a data-shape assumption bug.

items.question: Product wants the offline banner to say: Saved. Will sync within 5 minutes of reconnecting. Engineering can queue writes with Background Sync. Can you make that promise?
items.answer: No. Background Sync lets the browser retry queued work when connectivity returns, but browsers limit the number of retries and the execution time of each attempt, and the service worker itself can be stopped between attempts. Periodic background sync is browser-controlled, not a schedule the app owns. The honest UI states what is saved locally and that sync will be attempted, and the system must tolerate the attempt never succeeding.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that a background API is a scheduler. Every offline sync primitive on the web is best-effort and browser-governed, so any copy that names a time or guarantees delivery is a promise the platform cannot keep.

items.question: The outbox replays queued POSTs when the network returns. During the offline period, the server already accepted the same change from another device. What must have existed before that replay was ever enabled?
items.answer: Two things, decided before enabling queued mutations: idempotent writes, so replaying an operation cannot create a duplicate side effect, and a defined conflict resolution policy, so a replay that collides with newer server state has a known outcome instead of an undefined one. The queue is the easy part; the semantics of replay are what make offline writes safe.
items.trap: The naive design treats sync as replay the queue in order. Without idempotency, a retry after a partially completed request doubles the effect; without a conflict policy, the last writer silently wins or the request errors with no product answer for the user.

items.question: Design asks for the iOS and Android apps to be pixel-identical, citing brand consistency. How do you respond as the engineer responsible for the React Native app?
items.answer: Push back on identical pixels, not on consistency. The goal is a consistent product contract: the same capabilities, flows, and quality, implemented in ways that respect each platform. Keyboard behavior, permissions, navigation, accessibility, and the system back button all differ by platform, and forcing them to match one platform's conventions usually degrades the app on the other. Isolate the genuine differences behind platform APIs, platform-specific files, or small adapter components so the shared core stays clean.
items.trap: The naive framing treats cross-platform as one design rendered twice. Chasing pixel identity couples the app to whichever platform was designed first and produces an app that feels wrong everywhere else, while the consistency users actually notice is behavioral.

items.question: A codebase has Platform.OS === 'ios' checks scattered through 30 components and several business-logic modules. Refactoring is labeled nice to have. Why is it actually a correctness and velocity problem?
items.answer: Every scattered check multiplies the platform matrix the team must test and turns platform differences into invisible branches of business logic. The fix is a small platform seam: platform-specific files, Platform.select for values, and adapter components that expose one interface and hide the split. Platform behavior is then validated once at the seam instead of being rediscovered in every feature.
items.trap: The naive view is that inline platform checks are just style noise. In practice they leave both platforms partially untested, because each run exercises only one branch, and every new platform capability must be threaded through dozens of call sites instead of one adapter.

items.question: Leadership approved the New Architecture migration because removing the bridge makes the app faster. Six weeks after migrating, startup and scroll metrics are flat. Explain what the team misunderstood.
items.answer: The New Architecture replaces asynchronous bridge serialization with JSI-based interop and adds Fabric, which enables capabilities such as synchronous layout access. Those are capabilities, not automatic speedups: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring to benefit and that serialization may never have been the app's bottleneck. If the pre-migration profile showed the time going elsewhere, for example JS execution or native rendering, removing serialization cannot move those numbers.
items.trap: The naive model says the bridge was the cost, so removing it must be the win. The bridge was one cost among several; without a profile proving serialization dominated, flat metrics after migration are the expected outcome, not a failed migration.

items.question: The migration plan says: if New Architecture causes regressions, we will flip back to the old architecture. What is fragile about that rollback plan?
items.answer: It assumes the old architecture is still available on the React Native release you ship. The safe wording is a tested fallback only if the chosen release supports it. On releases where the old architecture is gone, there is nothing to flip back to, so the plan must instead be gradual rollout with crash and performance telemetry, and a halt procedure that stops the rollout rather than reverting the architecture.
items.trap: The naive plan treats the architecture toggle as a permanent escape hatch. Once the shipped React Native version no longer offers the old architecture, the rollback becomes a downgrade of the entire framework, which is a different and much riskier operation.

items.question: The team hit a wall: the app needs a native library, and Expo Go cannot load it. The proposal on the table is to eject to bare React Native. What is usually the better move, and why?
items.answer: Usually the better move is a development build: a build of your own project that includes the native libraries, produced through Expo's app configuration and prebuild pipeline. Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment, so its limits are the wall, not Expo itself. Ejecting to direct native ownership is justified by bespoke Gradle or Xcode integration or unusual native modules, not by the mere need for a native library.
items.trap: The naive syllogism is: Expo Go cannot do X, therefore Expo cannot do X, therefore eject. The wall is the playground, not the toolchain, and ejecting trades away repeatable native configuration and the managed build pipeline to solve a problem a development build already solves.

items.question: In an Expo project using Continuous Native Generation, a developer hand-edits the generated Xcode project to add a build setting. What happens to that edit, and where should the change live instead?
items.answer: The native projects are generated, so a hand edit can be overwritten the next time the native projects are regenerated. The change belongs in the app configuration layer that drives generation, so the native project stays reproducible from source. If the setting cannot be expressed there, that is the signal to evaluate whether this specific customization justifies direct native ownership of the project.
items.trap: The naive mental model treats android/ and ios/ as the source of truth, as in a bare project. Under CNG they are build output: editing them works until the next regeneration silently discards the change, which is the worst kind of failure because it surfaces far from its cause.

items.question: Stakeholders saw Chrome's install prompt on Android and now ask for the same one-tap flow on iPhone. What do you tell them, and what does that mean for the product design?
items.answer: On iOS and iPadOS there is no browser install prompt: users add the app manually through the browser share menu, and supported display modes and capabilities differ from desktop and Android. So the install journey must be platform-aware: detect or explain the platform-specific path, keep the core journey functional in a plain tab as progressive enhancement, and set the metric accordingly, for example guided add-to-home-screen completion on iOS rather than prompt acceptance.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that installation is a web capability that behaves uniformly across browsers. It is a per-platform experience, so copying the Android flow onto iOS produces instructions that do not match what the user sees and a funnel that looks broken.

items.question: The PWA passes QA in the browser tab, but stakeholders report the installed app looks and behaves differently. Why must the installed window be tested as its own target?
items.answer: Installation can give the app a separate window with its own display mode, and supported display modes and capabilities differ from the browser and across platforms. Assumptions that hold in a tab, such as browser chrome and navigation affordances, may not hold in the installed window. The installed experience therefore needs its own test pass, and storage, push, background behavior, and update UX should be verified on every supported browser rather than assumed native-equivalent.
items.trap: The naive view is that the installed app is the same page in a different frame. It is a distinct runtime context per platform, so bugs that only exist there, and capabilities that only differ there, are invisible to browser-only QA.

items.question: The app works perfectly on the office network, but Apple review rejects it for failing to load content. The submission is complete and uses only public APIs. What environmental condition did testing miss?
items.answer: Apple requires submissions to work on IPv6-only networks. A backend or dependency that still assumes IPv4 can pass every internal test on a dual-stack office network and fail review. Reproduce it by testing on an IPv6-only network before submitting, and recheck the current App Review guidelines for every release because the rules change.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that if it loads on our network, it loads on the internet. Review runs under conditions most offices never exercise by default, so network compatibility has to be tested explicitly, not inferred from local success.

items.question: The release plan uploads a single universal APK to Google Play. What is wrong with that submission format?
items.answer: Google Play uses Android App Bundles: you upload the signed bundle and Play generates device-optimized APKs from it. A universal APK ships every density and architecture to every device, which bloats the download, and it is not the submission format Play's current requirements expect. Bundle, sign, and let Play do the per-device splitting.
items.trap: The naive plan treats the APK built for internal testing as the release artifact. The bundle exists precisely so devices download only what they need, and submitting the universal APK throws that away while colliding with Play's submission requirements.

mcqs.question: A responsive layout is verified at 375px and 768px and looks correct at both. What is the most likely remaining gap?
options: Intermediate and landscape widths: breakpoints are snapshots, and fluid sizing must hold at every width between them
Nothing significant: if the two most common device classes pass, the layout is validated
Only widths above the largest breakpoint, since the 375px check already covers all narrow screens
Orientation does not need testing because media queries handle it automatically
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the guidance is to validate at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths, because a layout that works only at two breakpoint snapshots can still fail between them, which is exactly where landscape phones sit. The strongest distractor is option 2: device-class snapshot testing feels thorough but says nothing about the continuum of widths and orientations between and beyond the two checked points.

mcqs.question: You build a horizontal drag carousel on mobile web. During a drag the browser sometimes takes over and starts scrolling vertically instead. What is the correct fix?
options: Declare touch-action on the drag region (for example none, or pan-y if vertical scroll should remain) so the browser knows which gestures the region owns
Call event.preventDefault() inside every pointermove handler to cancel the scrolling
Attach non-passive touchstart listeners and cancel all touch events globally on the page
Filter handlers to pointerType === 'touch' only and ignore mouse and pen events
mcqs.explanation: Correct: with Pointer Events, the browser decides whether it may pan or zoom from the region's touch-action property, so you declare what the region owns instead of cancelling everything globally (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Pointer_events). The strongest distractor is option 2: preventDefault inside a pointer handler does not control browser panning, which is why the takeover keeps happening despite the cancellation attempts.

mcqs.question: During a Pointer Events drag, the pointer moves fast and leaves the element's bounds; pointermove events stop arriving at the original target. What keeps the drag alive?
options: setPointerCapture(event.pointerId) on the element at drag start, so subsequent events stay targeted to it even outside its bounds
Attaching a pointermove listener to document and manually hit-testing every move
Setting touch-action: none on the entire page
Calling event.stopPropagation() in the pointerdown handler
mcqs.explanation: Correct: pointer capture keeps subsequent events targeted to the capturing element even if the pointer leaves it, and it should be released on completion or cancellation. The strongest distractor is option 2: a document-level listener with manual hit-testing reimplements capture badly, because it still needs capture semantics to survive fast moves and to receive the events that matter during the drag.

mcqs.question: Which set correctly names the current Core Web Vitals and their recommended good thresholds?
options: LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.1
FCP within 1.8 seconds, FID at or below 100 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.1
LCP within 2.5 seconds, TTI within 3.8 seconds, CLS at or below 0.1
LCP within 1.2 seconds, INP at or below 200 milliseconds, CLS at or below 0.25
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the current Core Web Vitals are LCP for loading (2.5s), INP for interactivity (200ms), and CLS for visual stability (0.1), evaluated at the 75th percentile (web.dev: https://web.dev/articles/vitals). The strongest distractor is option 2: FCP and FID are real metrics and FID was the predecessor interactivity metric, but neither is part of the current Core Web Vitals set.

mcqs.question: Field data shows an INP regression on mobile but not on desktop, and you cannot reproduce it on your development machine. What is the correct next step?
options: Segment the field data by mobile device and route, use lab tooling to reproduce the likely cause, ship a fix, and confirm in field data again
Close the investigation: a performance issue that cannot be reproduced locally is not real
Apply every optimization available: memoize all components and defer all scripts, then watch the metric
Report only the desktop score, since that is what most stakeholders use
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the workflow is to segment field data by mobile device and page or route, reproduce the likely cause with lab tooling, ship an experiment, and compare field data after rollout, keeping real-user monitoring because lab results are not a substitute for field measurement. The strongest distractor is option 3: shotgun optimization changes many variables at once, so even if the metric moves you learn nothing about the cause, and it risks new regressions.

mcqs.question: In a React Native FlatList, tapping a row updates selectedId in parent state, but the previously selected row never visually deselects. data did not change. Why?
options: FlatList is a PureComponent: values outside data that affect rendering must arrive through changed props, so pass extraData={selectedId}
The list needs getItemLayout so rows re-render at the new selection
keyExtractor must include the selection state so each row gets a fresh key
Each row must be wrapped in React.memo with default props
mcqs.explanation: Correct: FlatList is a PureComponent, so a re-render only happens when its props change; selection lives outside data, so it must be passed as extraData (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/flatlist). The strongest distractor is option 3: baking selection into keys does force an update, but keys are identity, so every affected row remounts, losing row state and animations instead of updating in place.

mcqs.question: Product asks for the offline banner copy: Your changes will sync automatically within 5 minutes of reconnecting. What is the most accurate engineering response?
options: We can queue writes and retry them, but we cannot promise a time: Background Sync retries are limited, service workers can be stopped, and periodic sync is browser-controlled
Yes: Background Sync guarantees delivery once the network returns
Yes, if we set a timer in the service worker with setInterval
No, nothing can ever run in the background on the web
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Background Sync can retry short work but browsers limit retries and execution time, service workers can be stopped, and periodic background sync is browser-controlled rather than a guaranteed schedule, so the UI must never promise that a background task will definitely run at a particular time (MDN: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Progressive_web_apps/Guides/Offline_and_background_operation). The strongest distractor is option 2: it converts a best-effort retry mechanism into a delivery guarantee the platform does not offer.

mcqs.question: A team porting a web app to React Native assumes their existing DOM manipulation and CSS will keep working. Which statement reflects React Native's actual rendering model?
options: React components describe the UI, but core components map to native platform views, not browser DOM elements, so web CSS and browser APIs cannot be assumed to exist
The app renders inside a system web view, so existing DOM code keeps working after a small polyfill
React components are compiled to native source code at build time, so there is no JavaScript at runtime
The browser DOM is emulated on top of native views, so most web APIs work with minor differences
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the JavaScript side contains components and application logic while native projects bundle that JavaScript and render native components, so a web CSS or browser API must never be assumed (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/docs/components-and-apis). The strongest distractor is option 2: it describes a web-view approach, not React Native, whose core components map to real native views.

mcqs.question: After migrating to React Native's New Architecture, a team is surprised that startup time did not improve. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Serialization over the old bridge was probably not their bottleneck, and the app may need refactoring to benefit; the New Architecture enables capabilities rather than guaranteeing speedups
The migration was incomplete: JSI benefits require rewriting the components in C++
The old bridge is still running in parallel and must be deleted manually
Startup is always dominated by the bridge, so the measurement itself must be wrong
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the official guidance warns that an app may need refactoring and that serialization may not have been its bottleneck, so JSI-based interop and Fabric are capabilities, not automatic performance wins (React Native: https://reactnative.dev/architecture/landing-page). The strongest distractor is option 4: it denies the measurement instead of questioning the assumption, and it is exactly the belief that led the team to expect a guaranteed speedup.

mcqs.question: A team using Expo Go for daily development needs to integrate a third-party native library. What is the recommended move?
options: Move from Expo Go to a development build, which can include native libraries and production-like behavior
Eject to bare React Native immediately, because Expo cannot use native modules
Stay on Expo Go and mock the native library in development
Rebuild the app natively in Swift and Kotlin
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Expo Go is a limited playground, not the production development environment, so the move is a development build when native libraries or production-like behavior matter (Expo: https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/overview/). The strongest distractor is option 2: it is the classic eject myth; needing a native library is a limitation of the playground, not of the toolchain, and an Expo app is still a React Native app.

mcqs.question: Stakeholders want the same one-tap install prompt flow on iPhone that Chrome shows on Android. What is accurate?
options: On iOS and iPadOS there is no browser install prompt; users add the app manually through the browser share menu, so the flow must be platform-aware
Safari fires the same install prompt event as Chrome, so the flow can be reused
iOS supports install prompts only for apps with a paid Apple Developer account
iOS PWAs cannot be installed at all
mcqs.explanation: Correct: on iOS and iPadOS there is no browser install prompt and users add the app manually through the share menu, with display modes and capabilities that differ from desktop and Android, so installation should be productized as progressive enhancement with a platform-specific path (web.dev: https://web.dev/learn/pwa/installation). The strongest distractor is option 2: it assumes install UX is a uniform web capability, which is precisely the misconception that produces broken iOS funnels.

mcqs.question: What submission format does Google Play use for new app releases, and what does it do?
options: Android App Bundle: you upload the signed bundle and Play generates device-optimized APKs from it
A universal APK containing every density and architecture
An IPA package signed with the upload key
A signed release APK; App Bundles are optional and only for large teams
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Google Play uses Android App Bundles to generate device-optimized APKs, and requires signing (Google Play: https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9859152). The strongest distractor is option 2: a universal APK is what internal testing builds produce, but shipping it to the store sends every device all code and assets and does not match Play's submission requirements.

scenarios.prompt: This drag handle works with a mouse on desktop but misbehaves on touch: the browser sometimes scrolls instead of dragging, fast drags lose the element, and after a failed drag the handle stays stuck until the next tap. Find the bugs and rewrite the interaction.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Three defects, all touch-specific. First, gesture ownership: the code never declares touch-action, so on touch the browser is free to take over the drag for its own panning, which is why the page scrolls instead. preventDefault inside the pointer handlers does not control browser panning; the fix is a CSS declaration on the handle, touch-action: none for a pure drag, or pan-y if vertical page scrolling should survive while horizontal drags are custom. Second, event targeting: without pointer capture, a fast drag leaves the handle's bounds and pointermove retargets to whatever element the pointer is over, so the drag dies mid-gesture. Call handle.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId) in pointerdown and release it in the cleanup paths. Third, the missing end state: when the browser reclaims the gesture it fires pointercancel, not pointerup, so the move listener is never removed and the handle appears stuck. Handle pointercancel exactly like pointerup: remove the listener, release capture, and reset visual state. A corrected version: in pointerdown, setPointerCapture and attach move; in a shared end() function used by both pointerup and pointercancel, remove the listener and release capture if held. Keep move handlers small and only update the visual state that must change. Finally, a drag is a spatial gesture, so pair it with a semantic alternative (buttons or a slider) so the action is not gesture-only, and test with mouse, pen, and touch rather than pointerType checks unless device-specific behavior is genuinely needed.
rubric: Identifies touch-action as the mechanism that declares which browser gestures the region owns, and knows preventDefault in pointer handlers does not stop panning
Uses setPointerCapture on pointerdown and releases it on completion, explaining why fast drags otherwise lose the target
Treats pointercancel as a required end state alongside pointerup, and explains that the browser reclaiming the gesture is what fires it
Keeps move handling minimal and mentions a keyboard or semantic alternative for the action
Tests across mouse, pen, and touch instead of filtering on pointerType without cause

scenarios.prompt: Users report two bugs in this list: (1) tapping a row updates selection on some rows but the previously selected row often stays highlighted, and (2) after a fast scroll, the list lands on the wrong message. Row bodies can wrap to two or three lines. Explain both bugs and fix the component.
scenarios.modelAnswer: Bug 1 is a PureComponent prop problem. FlatList is a PureComponent, so it only re-renders when its props change. Tapping a row changes selectedId in the parent, but data does not change, so from the list's perspective nothing it watches has changed and rows keep stale selection visuals. The fix is to pass the outside value as a changed prop: extraData={selectedId}. Do not fix it by baking selection into keyExtractor: keys are identity, and changing them remounts rows, destroying row state and animations. While here, also stabilize renderItem and row props: the inline closure and the inline onPress are recreated every render, which works against keeping unrelated state from redrawing cells; hoist renderItem or memoize it and pass a stable onPress callback. Bug 2 is a geometry contract violation. getItemLayout is only valid for fixed-size rows: it lets the list skip measurement by trusting the declared length and offset. Row bodies wrap to two or three lines, so real heights exceed 64, and every offset after a tall row is wrong; the list scrolls to computed positions that no longer match content, which shows up as landing on the wrong message. Either constrain rows to a true fixed height (for example, clamped or truncated bodies) or remove getItemLayout and let the list measure. Before tuning anything else, profile to confirm where the time actually goes, and validate the fix on a representative lower-end Android device rather than a simulator, because window sizes tuned on a simulator can blank content on real devices or waste memory.
rubric: Diagnoses bug 1 through FlatList being a PureComponent and fixes it with extraData, not key hacks
Diagnoses bug 2 as getItemLayout's fixed-geometry contract being violated by variable-height rows
Keeps renderItem and row props stable instead of recreating closures each render
Profiles before tuning knobs and adjusts windowing only against device measurements
Validates on a representative lower-end Android device, not only a simulator

scenarios.prompt: Review this service worker for a PWA that must show reasonably fresh data and safely sync user edits made offline. What does it get wrong, and how should the offline behavior be designed instead?
scenarios.modelAnswer: The fetch handler applies cache-first to every API request. Cache-first favors speed but serves potentially stale assets, so API data cached once is replayed indefinitely: users see old data even when online, with no freshness signal and no fallback policy. The fix is a per-resource strategy: network-first for API data, falling back to the cache when the network fails, and cache-first only where staleness is acceptable, such as versioned static assets. The UI should also expose freshness, so cached responses are presented as what they are. The sync handler has the more dangerous bugs. First, replay is not idempotent: if a POST reaches the server but the response is lost, or the sync is retried, the same edit is applied twice. Each queued operation needs an idempotency mechanism so replaying it cannot duplicate the side effect. Second, there is no conflict policy: the server may have newer state from another device, and the code has no defined outcome for that collision; conflict resolution must be decided before queued mutations are enabled. Third, the loop is all-or-nothing: one failed fetch rejects the waitUntil, the remaining operations never run, and because browsers limit Background Sync retries and execution time, and the service worker can be stopped between attempts, the queue can strand. Each operation should be attempted and persisted independently, with per-op error handling. Finally, the product copy around this must never promise that a background task will run at a particular time: periodic sync is browser-controlled, retries are limited, and the UI must tolerate failure while showing what is saved locally and what is pending sync.
rubric: Rejects cache-first for API data and chooses a per-resource strategy, network-first for freshness with cache fallback
Identifies non-idempotent replay as the critical safety bug and requires idempotent writes
Requires a defined conflict resolution policy before queued mutations are enabled
Makes the sync loop per-operation and tolerant of partial failure instead of all-or-nothing
Refuses to promise background execution timing in the UI and exposes pending-sync state

scenarios.prompt: At 600px in landscape the cards overflow horizontally; at 320px they almost fit but the text is cramped; between 780px and 1000px the row is mostly empty space. Redesign the responsive approach and describe how you would validate it.
scenarios.modelAnswer: The root problem is device-snapshot thinking: one fixed card width (480px) plus one breakpoint at a single phone width (375px), so every width that is not exactly those two points gets a compromised layout. The redesign starts from content and fluid sizing: replace the fixed card width with flexible tracks, for example a grid with auto-fill and minmax so the column count adapts continuously to the available space, or flexbox with percentage-based cards that wrap. Make the images responsive so they scale with their container instead of carrying a fixed 960px width, and keep text readable at the smallest widths rather than merely fitting. If this card is reused in contexts with different available widths (page grid versus sidebar), give the component its own breakpoint with a container query instead of inheriting the page's device media queries. Validation is where the original approach failed: test at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths, in portrait and landscape, with real content (long names, missing images), not just the two popular device widths; a layout that works at two snapshots can still fail between them. Treat touch targets and readability as requirements of the mobile pass, and measure real mobile users separately in field data, since the Core Web Vitals guidance recommends segmenting results by mobile and desktop rather than reading one aggregate.
rubric: Replaces fixed pixel card widths with fluid sizing and flexible layout primitives (grid or flexbox)
Makes images responsive rather than fixed-size, and keeps text readable at the smallest widths
Reaches for container queries when the component, not the page, needs its own breakpoint
Validates at narrow, wide, and intermediate widths in both orientations with real content, not two device snapshots
Segments performance field data by mobile instead of relying on an aggregate score
